utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. I was informed there are a few preliminaries to deal with. I have a few as well. The first one, however, would be that the Chamber would appreciate if the -- yes, I first -- could I invite Madam Registrar to called the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The first one would be that if the Defence would start distributing the materials at such a time in the morning that the Chamber doesn't have to wait until it is done, that would be appreciated. Because we can't start without an usher, and if the usher is running around even after 9.00 to distribute materials, then that should have started earlier. Then the first issue. Mr. Jordash, on the 19th of January, you have requested that parts of your cross-examination of Witness Jovan Dimitrijevic on 18th of January would be made public, that was the parts that were in private session. You're hereby invited to give precise, from line here to line there, so that the Registry is better able to prepare for it once we've given an order, and for the Chamber to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we -- yes, and once you've done that, Mr. Jordash, of course the other parties are invited to review the references, the exact references, to the transcript so as to inform the Chamber whether they have any objection against those portions to become public. Then for the next item we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I give you an opportunity, Ms. Marcus, to address the Chamber, I would like to put on the record a matter which was dealt with in private session which could have been dealt with in open session. That is, that the Stanisic Defence has informed the Chamber that it will not call Witness DST-081. Ms. Marcus, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution would like to note that we are still not in receipt of the Simatovic proposed military expert report in English. We are increasingly concerned about the delays in receipt of this report, in particular in light of the length. We'd like to emphasise that the report, when provided, should include the -- in the footnotes the references to exhibit numbers, 65 ter numbers, or other reference information so as not to delay the process of reviewing this report even further. And the last issue I'd like to raise, Your Honour, is that we appreciate the agreement with Simatovic Defence to provide us with the documents for upcoming witnesses seven days in advance. I'd just like it to be clear that the seven day in advance is for English translations. For us to receive the B/C/S documents seven days in advance and the English translations 24 hours in advance is basically the same thing as providing the documents at the last minute. We had a great deal of difficulty, I think, with the past two witnesses with respect to translations, and we would request that that agreement apply to the English translations, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With regard to the first issue raised by my learned colleague, we still have not yet received the translation of the expert report. We were promised to receive the report by the middle of this month. I informed you of the fact we haven't yet received it. The -- and as soon as it is available, we will provide the report. As far as the footnotes are concerned, that should accompany the report. We are working hard to identify the documents, and we will inform the Prosecution of the results. We are trying to tie up all the documents in the file to include them in the expert report, and this will facilitate the work for all the parties, including the Prosecution, in the proceedings. We did the same for the police expert. We provided our colleagues with the report, with the footnotes, including P, D, and 65 ter numbers. Unfortunately some translations are still missing. But everything that still concerns that report has been submitted for translation, and we expect these translations to be available very soon, both us and for the Prosecution, of course. As far as the second issue raised by my learned colleague is concerned, the issue that concerns the translation of documents used with witnesses, we are trying to act as diligently as possible with regard to that matter too. It is to a certain extent outside our control. Unfortunately, when the proofing of the witness has been completed, sometimes it proves to be necessary to produce some additional documents, as a result of which concern problems are created. But we are really trying to respect the seven-day deadline. But unfortunately certain things are beyond our control. It all depends on the capacity of the translation unit. But I believe that no one puts into dispute our goodwill with regard to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see there are a lot of good intentions. Whether that would do is matters still to be seen. I don't know whether that saying also exists in the English language, but in my own language there is a saying that good intentions pave the way to a place where you would rather not want to be. Could you please keep that in mind, that the result is what counts. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same expression exists in our language, Your Honour. But I believe that this will not be the case, as far as our efforts are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I just wanted to point at that good intentions do not always lead to the kind of success we are all aware is needed. Ms. Marcus, I leave it to that for the time being. Apparently in the many languages similar expressions do exist. Then, if there's no -- Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We do have one additional matter that pertains to the next witness, if we may proceed with that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the next witness, the Simatovic Defence disclosed a notice to a large quantity of materials this past week, materials that are not on the Defence exhibit list. These materials included an extensive amount of video footage provided on CDs that contain a programme which allows us to view the videos but not process them in our system. These videos also appear highly edited; at this time we do not know by whom. Examples of these edits include the following: During a speech by the witness which is uploaded as 65 ter 2D1016.1, and appears to be from the 11th of October, 1995, there is an edit after the witness states: "On this day five years ago." And we do not know what is said after that comment. Also, the videos include an interview with the witness and he is asked by an English-speaking reporter: "What do you have to say about the allegations of ethnic cleansing in Sanski Most?" And the answer is cut. The Prosecution finds these edits to be relevant and curious. We would ask that the Simatovic Defence provide us with the complete unedited videos in an acceptable format. The Prosecution further requests that if the Simatovic Defence is going to use these videos and they're allowed to be added onto their exhibit list in their present form, that they be marked for identification pending the receipt of the unedited videos. Next: We also received notice of five documents that are to be added. These are 2D904, 2D905, 2D906, 2D1018, and 2D1019. We received the translations to 2D905 and 906 this morning. Based on the threshold provided and although there is significantly late notice, including late notice of substance related to this witness's testimony in a proofing note yesterday, we do believe that it would be most efficient to allow the -- the documents to be added to the Defence exhibit list at this time. However, the Prosecution does reserve some issues with respect to the eventual admission of these documents. There were also photos that were provided to us. These are 2D1020, 2D1034, which -- it is our understanding that it was provided by the witness during proofing that past weekend. There is unknown information about these photos, although we do recognise the individuals who are present in the photos. For the basis of adding the photos to the Defence exhibit list, the Prosecution does not oppose it; however, we will further discuss some additional information with them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Editing the videos, Mr. Bakrac. Who edited the videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we received these videos from the witness and provided them to the Prosecution in the form that we received them. As far as I can see - I'm not certain about this, however - the witness said that these videos were made 16 years ago on VHS video tapes. And they were then transferred to DVDs. I have nothing against Mr. Weber's suggestion that they should retain MFI numbers and we could later try to obtain the original VHS tapes, if they exist, and we could then provide the Prosecution with these VHS tapes that I assume were used to make the DVDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know whether the Prosecution is that much interested in the original VHS if they are edited in the same way as what we find on the DVDs. If, however, the VHS copies are more extensive and then reduced when put on a DVD, then I can imagine that you would like to see the original material. But an answer to Mr. Weber's question is not there yet: Who edited it? And I think if the witness provides them, then the first question should be to the witness: who edited them; where the original material is. And another matter. When the accused is shown on the video to be speaking, then, of course, the admissibility of such evidence may relate to what kind of questions are put to the witness. If it is just to have in evidence some statements of the accused [sic], then, of course, if we do not know what the source is when the accused cannot be cross-examined on the statements he makes, that is a matter still to be considered perhaps. I also noticed that the amount of video material is considerable. And the Chamber will carefully look at how it is used. And, Mr. Bakrac, since it is your witness, videos should not play a role in leading the witness; so therefore, you are expected to do the same as we always expect a calling party to do, that is, to first see whether the evidence can be elicited without showing material. And only if that's not possible or if that does not -- or if that causes the need to further put to the witness some material, then, of course, that can be done. But please be aware that this kind of material requires a very precise and cautious approach, as far as eliciting evidence from a witness is concerned. It could not be to ask the witness: Have you ever seen this video? Of course he has, because he gave it to you. And then to say, "Okay, that's then the evidence," that's perhaps not the way we should proceed. Mr. Weber, I added even a few concerns to yours. Mr. Bakrac doesn't know who edited the video. Didn't you ask, Mr. Bakrac? Didn't you ask the witness where does it come from, who edited it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interpretation I am receiving is changed. If I have understood the witness correctly, the video was made by someone -- in fact, could we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, while waiting for the witness, I need to apologise to you because this morning the usher was busy distributing documents. Yesterday in the course of the proofing of this witness we spoke about certain photographs. The witness then called home and asked his wife to provide him with an additional three photographs, and our assistant, our case manager, had to upload these photographs, which is why we were late in distributing these transcripts. I do apologise if the Chamber had to wait as a result of this event. In future, we will make sure that this does not happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pelevic, if I'm well informed. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Pelevic. Mr. Pelevic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Bakrac, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Kindly introduce yourself for the record. What is your name and when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Borislav Pelevic. I was born on the 22nd November, 1956, in the village of Bublje municipality, Orahovac, in Kosovo and Metohija in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, kindly tell us what is your profession or what is your educational background.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I have a Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly what is your educational background.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the school of economics in Pristina. I obtained my masters in Pristina. And I obtained my Ph.D. from the school of sport and tourism in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we have to make pauses between questions and answers since we speak the same language. My question needs to be interpreted first before you can start giving your answer. Therefore, I would kindly ask you to wait a little before you start replying to my questions.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I think that already for the reasons you indicated, part of the answer is not on the record. You said you obtained your masters in Pristina. And then you gave additional information. Could you please repeat that additional information. I think I heard Novi Sad being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that I had obtained my Ph.D. in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think you also referred to the subjects.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I had graduated from the school of sports and tourism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, could you please tell us where are you currently employed.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Currently I work as am MP in the Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In addition to being an MP, do you have some other duties? And if that is the case, could you please tell us what duties are those.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I teach at the school of sports and health in Belgrade. Also I'm the president of the kick-box association of Serbia. I'm also a vice-president of the world kick-box organisation and the president of the referee committee of the kick-box organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You have just told us that you are the president of the referee committee of the kick-box organisation. Which organisation is that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: It is the World Kickboxing Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, please tell us something else. We will skip some parts of your educational and profession background, and we'll move straightly on to some very specific subjects. At one point in the 1990s you joined the Serbian Volunteer Guards. When was that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Serbian Volunteer Guard on the 10th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how you joined. What motivated you? How did you join the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: My brother was a volunteer in the JNA before me. We had agreed as a family that he would be the first one to join as a volunteer, and then when he returned it was my turn. However, when he returned from the front line, he told me that he was not very satisfied with the organisation of the then-JNA. He told me that there was a visible lack of discipline there, and he told me that I should join the Serbian Volunteer Guard. He saw them in action on the front line and he thought that that would be something for me as a former athlete. That they are the real army. That's how I decided to volunteer. I went to the recruiting office of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in Belgrade, I volunteered, and then two days later I was transported in a van to Erdut where the headquarters was, as well as the training centre of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you alone in that van or was there anybody else with you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: There was me and two other volunteers. They were also recruited.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How were you dressed? And where did you cross the border from Serbia to Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I wore civilian clothes. We crossed the border across the bridge near Bogojevo, very close to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you stopped at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that there was a soldier, a JNA soldier. He just saluted the driver, and we crossed without ever being checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Erdut, who received you there? And what happened next? Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: We went through the gate. A man, a tall man who came across as having authority, waited for us at the entrance into the centre. And then he first asked me, Are you that master of arts or sciences? And I said yes. And then he sent the other two to the barber because they had very long hair. I did not have to have my hair cut. I had short hair already. And he ordered me to share a room with a sergeant from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, when you volunteered you had a master's degree in economics.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you employed? And if that was the case, where?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I was the general manager of the Sportinvest public company based in Belgrade. And also I was the president of the kick-box federation of Serbia. I apologise, the kick-box federation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I again insist on making a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, when you arrived in Erdut, did you have to fill out a form? And if that was the case, who asked you to do that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I filled out a form. There was a clerk there who asked me to it that. Later on I learned that his name was Jovan Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the day when you arrived in Erdut, were you issued with a uniform? And if that was the case, what kind of a uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was issued with a woolen olive-drab uniform that had previously been worn by the soldiers of the JNA. For the first few days, all of us volunteers were issued with that kind of uniform. And also those who served a sentence, guard members, also used to wear it. We called it a partisan uniform, and that's why, when we were mocked, we were also referred to as partisans.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say for the benefit of the booths that in the next couple of minutes I'm going to up 2D1017.1 which is a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, when you were issued with that so-called partisan uniform, were you also issued with any weapons during those first couple of days?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What were your initial duties when you first joined the guards, when you volunteered, and when you arrived in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: On the following morning, I was ordered to clean the barracks perimeter from cigarette butts, and that's what I did for the first three days after my arrival in Erdut. That's what I did the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I asked my sergeant, who was also my roommate, to arrange a meeting with my company commander. My company commander was an officer, and I told him that I had not come to Erdut to clean the perimeter from cigarette butts but to fight for the freedom of my people. If I was not given a good uniform and good weapons and if I was not sent for training, it was my intention to leave Erdut and to go back to Belgrade. I told him all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What happened next? Were you issued with weapons? Were you issued with another type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: He told me that he would have a word with Commander Arkan about that, and that in the course of the day he would keep me posted. In the course of the day, I was still cleaning. He approached me and told me that the commander approved my membership, my regular membership in the company, and that he agreed that I should start training.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you issued with the weapons and did your uniform change after that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was issued with an olive-drab overall, a pair of boots, and I was also issued with an automatic rifle, M-70.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said an olive-drab overall. I would like to call up a video-clip, and I would invite your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can play this video-clip without sound. For everybody's benefit, please pay attention to the events and the faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then after the video-clip is played, I will have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like called up 2D1017.1. This is from the Prosecutor's disclosure list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could just have the full ERN, the VOOO number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. VOOO-2253.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, do you recognise -- or, rather, do you know anything about this event depicted in the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: This is General Bratic's burial, who had formally been the commander of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when he was the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, up to then, and who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he was killed. I only know that he was killed on the Trpinje road. I learned that subsequently. It was all over the media. But I know that he was succeeded by General Andrija Biorcevic as the commander of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you recognise Mr. Raznjatovic, did you recognise his uniform, and did you recognise the person he was standing next to during the burial?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised him wearing the olive-drab overall that all of us wore. Absolutely the same kind. Next to him was the then-president of the Serbian region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Goran Hadzic. I recognised a few -- a couple of other highly-ranking officers. I saw General Blagoje Adzic standing behind the flag. He was the deputy chief of the General Staff at the time. And the person who spoke was Goran Hadzic. And the person still on the screen is Lieutenant-General Zivota Panic. I believe that he was the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time, which means that he occupied the highest ranking position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender 2D1017.1 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection if it's admitted with the transcript provided, since the transcript does provide some additional information as to where this funeral occurred, things like that, which I imagine is not in dispute if it's being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's played without audio, so therefore it might be a bit difficult to introduce something into evidence the Chamber hasn't seen. Unless the parties would agree that the comment provides the additional information as to location and time, we would then consider ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Registry is not provided with the videos, so therefore it's difficult to have it in the e-court system if it's only on a -- played from a DVD, or I don't know how it works, but ... We reserve a number for this clip, and then during the break, Mr. Bakrac, you may explain to Madam Registrar what it is. Meanwhile, the parties are invited to see whether they can agree on either a transcript -- or if you agree on when this took place and where it took place, then, of course, that agreement could be put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me explain why we played a clip without the sound. I believe that we follow the common practice. What I mean with that is that the Trial Chamber tends not to like the commentary provided on those video-clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you in any way for it. It doesn't need an explanation. But Mr. Weber rightly points at the fact that we have no information about time and location. He suggests one way of introducing that information. There may be others as well. I left that to the parties during the break, which we'll take now. And we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any report as to the location and time of the last video we looked at?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, I'm not sure my microphone is working. Your Honour, we're still checking the exact date of the funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we had a look at the video. Tell me, after General Bratic was killed, who became the head of the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Andrija Biorcevic, lieutenant-general, became the head of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mentioned olive-green overalls. And you said the ones that you saw on Arkan, that you saw at the funeral, was the kind that you wore too. Do you know where these overalls were obtained, and how?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I couldn't know. I was just a recruit. But later I found out that we received the first uniforms from the JNA, or the Army of Yugoslavia in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any information according to which you received other things from the Army of Yugoslavia apart from the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received weapons and relevant equipment: ammunition, Zoljas, bombs or grenades, and Osas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "weapons," what do you have in mind? What kind of weapons did you in fact receive?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at the guards, there were various types of weapons there. There were automatic rifles, M-70 automatic rifles, and there were semi-automatic rifles as well. There were also perhaps four or five Hecklers, small automatic weapons, Hecklers and Kochs [as interpreted], that commander Arkan had on him, as well as a few other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know where Arkan and these officers obtained those Heckler & Koch weapons? And what kind of weapons are they, what are they used for?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Since I'm quite familiar with weapons, I found it quite surprising that some officers had automatic Heckler & Koch rifles with them, and naturally I was curious and asked my superiors where they these items were obtained from. They said they had been seized in an operation in the vicinity of Osijek, I believe. But since you've asked me what the purpose of such weapons is, I would say that these weapons aren't really used on the battle-field. It's more the case that special units in towns used these weapons. So the war-time weapons that were used the most in this war were automatic and semi-automatic rifles. Semi-automatic rifles were later excluded when we received other weapons from the JNA, or, rather, from the Army of Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you later tried to obtain information. When you became close to Mr. Arkan, did you find out how the Serbian Volunteer Guards and how Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, obtained these weapons from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I found out about this from three sources. From Commander Arkan, he was the first source. He told me that the weapons were obtained from the Army of Yugoslavia because that was the agreement he had reached with the minister of defence today, Tomislav Simovic. The second source was General Biorcevic. We became fairly good friends later on, and he confirmed this. And Ms. Dobrila Glisic was another source. She wrote a book on the events. She was the chef de cabinet for General Simovic, the minister of defence. And it so happens that she's a friend of the parents of my wife. The father of my wife was a neurosurgeon at the military medical academy, and he treated her son. So she told me about the meeting between the commander, Arkan, and General Tomislav Simovic, the minister of defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know who referred Arkan to General Simovic, the minister of defence of the Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know who referred him. Radmilo Bogdanovic did, when he was the Ministry of the Interior in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Arkan asked him for his assistance since they knew each other. And Radmilo Bogdanovic was an official in the Crvena Zvijezda football club. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was the leader for the Crvena Zvijezda fans. On that occasion they had to be in contact. He told him that some Crvena Zvijezda fans, together with himself, had decided to found the Serbian Volunteer Guards and go to the Slavonia battle-field. And he asked for the assistance in the form of weapons and equipment. Radmilo Bogdanovic said that this was not possible, and he referred him to the minister of defence, Tomislav Simovic. And this meeting was held and had the results that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you joined the guards in January 1992 as you said, from that point in time onwards when you were in Erdut did you receive any weapons, any additional weapons? And if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: As far as weapons themselves are concerned, large amounts did not regularly arrive. The situation was normal. But if there was a defective rifle or if a rifle was lost, then we would request that the TO based in Dalj provide us with weapons. But two or three times a week we requested that they provide us with ammunition, because a lot of ammunition was used for training, when the volunteers, the Serbian Volunteer Guards, were being trained. In one day one combatant would use at least 60 bullets, two clips. Then we asked the TO, the Territorial Defence, for ammunition. Not just ammunition, but also for Zoljas, hand-held rocket-launchers that could be used once. We also requested that they provide us with grenades, hand grenades. So this is the way in which we would obtain ammunition supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you came across automatic and semi-automatic rifles in Erdut. Were the semi-automatic rifles replaced at some point in time? If so, in what manner and how were they replaced? Who did this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: This occurred after a battle in which the Serbian Volunteer Guards captured six --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: eight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- tanks. Six of the tanks we handed over to the army immediately, and we kept two of them. The reason for keeping those two tanks is unknown to me since we didn't a tank corps or tank unit in the guards. But later I understood that commander Arkan did this quite skilfully. He wanted to exchange these two tanks for new automatic rifles so that the guards would no longer have these other weapons that weren't as good as automatic rifles. And this is what happened in agreement with General Andrija Biorcevic and his Chief of Staff, Bore Jovancevic [phoen]. An agreement was reached according to which a large amount of automatic rifles and accompanying equipment would be provided for those two tanks. So we gave them the PUP semi-automatic rifles, and in return we received "papovke" automatic rifles. There were no other significant changes from that point in time onwards when it comes to the weapons that the guards had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, when you mention the names of certain items, could you please slow down a bit so that the interpretation booths can translate what you are saying. When these captured tanks were exchanged for those weapons, tell me, were you already in the guards at the time or did this take place prior to that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No, that happened before I joined the guards. But I heard this from my colleagues, other volunteers. And later, Commander Arkan told me about this, as well as General Andrija Biorcevic, about some interesting situations that concerned that exchange. So they were very happy to go over that subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you joined the guards -- in fact, first - I do apologise - tell me, Do you know whether there was another way in which Arkan obtained uniforms for his troops; and, if so, could you briefly tell us how he obtained them and where he obtained them from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Commander Arkan always wanted his guards to be the best equipped guards. He wanted their units to be -- their uniforms to be better than the uniforms of those of everyone else in the battle-field. Part of the uniforms, part of the camouflage uniforms, were received from someone who donated them in Canada. But the quantity wasn't sufficient for all the guards, so one overall was taken to Novi Sad, to Stankamenac [phoen], a man called Stankamenac, and he used that uniform to make a certain number of camouflage uniforms. I know that some of those uniforms were also sewn in the Yumco factory in Kosovo and Metohija. I think it was in Kosovo Polje, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there also a shop where it was possible to openly buy certain equipment? And do you know whether Arkan went there to obtain certain supplies as well?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was such a shop, and I believe that the shop still exists. The name of the shop is Magnum, or perhaps it's called Army Shop today. You can buy equipment and uniforms, but now weapons. You can buy hunting knives, but not other weapons. I know that Commander Arkan bought just for the officers some very nice uniforms in that shop in Belgrade. He bought some knives and officer boots, so that the officers looked quite different from the ordinary soldiers, from us who were the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any other additional equipment obtained from that private shop?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, tell me -- or, rather, you described the first three days for us, and then you said that you were issued with a different type of uniform, which was a green overall, and that you were issued with an M-70 automatic rifle. What happened next? What did you do at the beginning of 1992 at the Erdut centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: As soon as I became a regular member of my unit, I started training, which lasted three months. Before completing their training, no volunteer could be sent to a front line or on a mission. My lieutenant noticed that I was in good shape. I was a karate master and I had trained other martial arts. Fifteen days into my stay, he asked me to be his assistant when it came to the physical training of not just the company, but the entire guard. Some 20 days later, therefore, I started training people. What I was impressed with in the guard was a high level of discipline. People were not allowed to consume alcohol. We showed a lot of respect to our superiors and vice versa; they respected us as well. So the entire atmosphere in the guards was really very good. I found it really very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you started training other people, what was the relationship between Arkan and the commander of the Novi Sad Corps? Did the latter ever come to the headquarters in Erdut? Did Arkan or perhaps you as well go to their staff, to the army staff? And if you did, why did you do so?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Biorcevic came several times while I was in Erdut. He paid the centre, the 101st Centre in Erdut a visit. And whenever he came, Commander Arkan lined up all of the guards. General Biorcevic saluted the volunteers as soon as he arrived in the centre. And the first thing he told us was, Comrade, soldiers, I salute you. That was the common salute in the former army. And then we would respond, God be with you. That was kind of sweet at first, but then he gave up on saluting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, did Arkan ever go to the Novi Corps Staff? If he did, do you know who he visited and why?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: General Biorcevic had some sort of a staff on a boat or on a ship. I believe that the name of that ship was either Kozara or Sutiska, I'm not sure. But it was either the name of a mountain or a river from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The commander would go there. On two occasions, when we became close, I went with him to that staff. And on one occasion, we also dined with Vladika, of Osijek and Dalj, Lukijan. Because we as guards repaired his church that the Croatian soldiers or volunteers had partly damaged. The restoration works lasted for about two months, and after their completion Vladika Lukijan invited Commander Arkan, myself, General Biornevic [phoen], and General Boro Ivanovic, the Chief of Staff of the Novi Sad Corps, to lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And how my last question on that topic. From the moment you arrived in Erdut, did you go on any joint missions with the army? And if that was the case, under whose command did you act?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I don't understand your question. Are you referring to the period before the real combat started; or are you referring to some smaller-sized actions that were carried out?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you joined the guards, did you hear that the Serbian Volunteer Guard carried out some operation in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, now I understand your question. I didn't at first. The Serbian Volunteer Guard together with the military carried out actions almost all over Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem. I would like to point out the Operation Luzac, where our guards launched an infantry attack and they were supported by the Army of Yugoslavia artillery and tanks, since we did not have any tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who was in command in those actions and operations? What can you tell us about the command function?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: We always received our orders from the corps commander of the Army of Yugoslavia. At first that was General Bratic. He was succeeded by General Biorcevic. And their inferiors, colonels, or lieutenant-colonel. However, no operation would be undertaken without the co-operation of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, that's something that you learned when you arrived there. From the moment you arrived, did you carry out any actions in 1992 together with the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, there were just a few smaller-sized operations. For example, we received information from the army that a ship on its way from Romania was carrying mercenaries for the Croatian army. We stopped that ship, we established that the allegations were true, and we ordered the captain to go back to Romania. That was an action that I participated in. And there were some other smaller ones, such as countering their scouts that infiltrated in our territory. We also sent our scouts to surveil their territory in depth. I always participated in those smaller actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, your centre in Erdut, who did it belong to? Can define that for us? When you arrived, when you saw the situation, did you learn what the name of the centre was and who that centre belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, I saw a big billboard at the very entrance into the centre, and the inscription on there was the 101st Training Centre of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, which means that it belonged to the Territorial Defence and its headquarters was in Dalj, a town very close to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic. Do you know who the commander of the Territorial Defence was when you arrived, the Territorial Defence of the autonomous region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. Because he often came to the training centre. His name was Radovan Stojicic, Badza. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence. And by virtue of that position he was our superior commander, because we were a Territorial Defence unit for the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, in the former Yugoslavia, the Territorial Defence was under whose jurisdiction? Not just one Territorial Defence, but all of the Territorial Defence forces, under whose jurisdiction were they?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Under the jurisdictions of the military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, the camp in Erdut, did there come a time when things changed? I apologise, I'll rephrase my question. First of all tell me, Do you know and can you define the relationship between Arkan and Radovan Stojicic, Badza?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I would say that their relationship was not as members of the military but as friends. Friends. Badza often came to our centre and the two of them forged a very sincere friendship with the common goal to defend the territory. Their relationship was fair and friendly, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, to your knowledge, did anybody come to the training centre in Erdut while you were there, or before you were there, as a representative of the MUP of Serbia or the state security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm sure that nobody did. There was quite a great detail of animosity between the guards and the MUP of Serbia and especially between the guards and the state security of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, is it true that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, once he stopped being the commander of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, somewhat later became an assistant minister of the MUP of Serbia and the chief of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a notorious fact. Everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain the difference for us. You said that Arkan was close to Radovan Stojicic, Badza, who later became what he did. And at the same time you're telling me that the Serbian Volunteer Guard, all of its members, and Arkan harboured quite a lot of animosity towards the MUP and the DB. How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you briefly. That animosity was due to the fact that we thought that the DB, i.e., the secret police and the police in general, saw Arkan as a person with a criminal record. That was our perception. And I don't think that our perception was far off. And it was sold to the media all the time. They wanted to undermine Commander Arkan's credibility and the guards' successes. But let me explain the nature of the relationship with Radovan Stojicic, Badza. As I've already told you, that relationship was created on the ground, in Slavonia. Badza was the commander of the Territorial Defence as well as the commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guard that was part of the Territorial Defence. So that friendship cannot -- does not -- must not be confused with Arkan's attitude towards the police and the DB. This was a very personal relationship, and that continued to exist all the way up to Badza's death. I really know a lot about that, and a distinction has to be made. Badza was an assistant minister of public security, not the secret police, and there's a distinction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, you said that you -- you claim that nobody from the MUP and especially not from the DB of Serbia came to our camp [as interpreted]. Did you ever doubt that there was somebody in the Erdut camp who could perhaps leak information to the MUP or the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: All secret services everywhere in the world try to infiltrate their own people into those spheres of life or those units that they want to monitor, check, or discredit. That's why we assumed that out of the 250 to 300 volunteers there must have been a spy or two. We were really not that naive not to doubt that. We had our suspicions about a volunteer who was a very brave soldier, a very intelligent and resourceful person; however, he arose our suspicions with his behaviour. He often made telephone calls, but not from the centre in Erdut but from the centre of the village. He often applied for leaves. And according to a story, in Belgrade he was once seen in front of the DB building. There was no way for us to confirm our suspicions, and it remains unproven to this day whether he was, indeed, a DB agent or not. However, out of the abundance of caution, he was expelled from the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like the Chamber to move into private session. I would like to ask Mr. Pelevic to try and remember the name of that person that he has just described for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we see 2D1033 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And while waiting for that: Mr. Pelevic, I believe that you brought this photograph with you when you came to The Hague. Be so kind as to tell me whether you can recognise the place where the photograph was taken. Can you remember the occasion and the time? And who are the individuals that we can see in the foreground?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Naturally. The person in the uniform is Commander Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. To his left, we see Mr. Goran Hadzic, the president of the Autonomous Region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem at the time. And to the right, the man in the black is Milan Milanovic, Mrgud, the deputy minister of defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the man in the black suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And can you remember when this photograph was taken, and on what occasion, if you know? And I do apologise, we failed to ask you where this photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The photograph was taken in the guards centre. It's the -- the compound itself. It's the training centre. And the photograph was taken on the occasion of the day on which the Serbian Volunteers Guard was formed, on the 10th of October, 1992. In the background you can see other individuals who were always present on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this photograph please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1033 will receive number D651, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, concerning this camp in Erdut, what was its capacity? How many members did you have in the guards?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Before we arrived, the camp in Erdut was a recruit centre for the Osijek Military District. So it had everything that a combat unit needed. It wasn't very big. It had a capacity of about 250 beds, but very often there were over 300 guards there, because they would use mattresses or sleeping bags instead of beds. They had a canteen, training grounds -- it had a canteen and training grounds, good dormitories, there was an office, a big warehouse. So everything that a large combat unit needed was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, did you take over responsibility for training the recruits at any point in time; and, if so, when did you do so?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To a certain extent I did assume responsibility for recruiting [as interpreted] the recruits, perhaps after two or two and a half months -- after I had been in the volunteer guards for two and two and a half months. I was good at martial arts, I was physically fit, I knew how to prepare troops, so I assumed responsibility for physical training, for training in martial arts. It was necessary to be very fit, because if a military unit -- if members of a military unit aren't fit, they can be very good shooters but that will serve no purpose because you need to be fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, how long did the recruits' training last?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, it lasted for three months. Only after they had been trained for three months was it possible for a volunteer to join the combat group and to participate in the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were the instructors who trained the recruits just members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, or did you have instructors who came from the outside too?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: When Legija arrived in the guards, that was in 1992, in April 1992, he was also appointed as an instructor since he had a lot of military experience. He had been sergeant in the Foreign Legion for four years, so he had such experience. We also had a colonel, an army colonel, a colonel from the JNA, and because of his rank we called him Puki, which is the abbreviation for "colonel," or "pukovnik." I don't know whether he had retired or whether he was an active-duty officer, but I do know that he wore a uniform that was different from the uniforms we had. He wore the uniform of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In order to be quite clear: Was he a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, or did he only appear from the outside in order to train the recruits?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No. He lived with us. He was a member of the guards. But he probably kept some of his habits from the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive training of any kind from members of the MUP of Republika Srbija or from any other MUP or from members of the state security in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No. That would have been quite unnatural. That never occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why do you say that that would have been abnormal?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the police and the stays security, given the nature of their work, are not military units, and they know nothing about warfare. Why should we be trained by them with regard to how to arrest someone or how to spy on someone? This is the work that is to be done by the DB or the MUP. We can only have instructors from military units; that's quite natural. So it wasn't necessary for us to have any such instructors from the DB or the MUP. And in my opinion they had no such instructors, no such experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, throughout the year 1992 did you provide training from [as interpreted] recruits or did you at any point in time leave Erdut; and if you did, when and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, I received an order from Commander Arkan. I was to select four of the best volunteers, soldiers, and to go to Knin, to a place called Kistanje, near Knin, where the Krka monastery had been located. It had been built in the thirteenth century by the sister of the Serbian tsar, Jelena. This monastery is near the border with Croatia, and from the surrounding hills the Croatian soldiers would often fire on the monastery. Since at the time Vladika Nikolaj was in the monastery, he had to flee from Sibenik, he asked Milan Martic to provide security and defend the monastery from attacks. Milan Martic referred him to Arkan, since he didn't have enough forces. That's what he later told me. He didn't have enough forces to provide security, and Commander Arkan sent me and four other soldiers under my command to go and defend the monastery, to arm the monks, to train them, to provide them physical training and training in shooting. I went there towards the end of March to carry out that task and I stayed there for perhaps 30 days, but not for more than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say towards the end of March, for the sake of the transcript, which year are we dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, did the Serbian Volunteer Guards carry out any operations during the time that you spent in the Krka monastery?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian Volunteer Guards at the beginning of April participated in the liberation of Bijeljina and Zvornik. Those were the two largest operations carried out by the Serbian Volunteer Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As far as I have understood, you weren't present, you didn't participate in those operations. When you returned in Erdut after 30 days, as you say, did you hear anything about the participation of the volunteer -- of the Serbian Volunteer Guards in the liberation of Bijeljina and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Naturally I heard certain things from my colleagues and from officers. And later, naturally, from Commander Arkan as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know how it is that the Serbian Volunteer Guards and Arkan went to Bijeljina and later on to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Volunteer Guards had been appealed to by Ms. Biljana Plavsic on behalf of the SDS, and they had been asked to prevent Muslim extremists who had already compiled a list of prominent Serbs in Bijeljina -- they were asked to prevent these Muslim extremists from assassinating Serbians on this list. I know about that because I had the document and there was a coded call. Biljana Plavsic asked the commander to act in such a way to defend these prominent individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In addition to this call that the commander received, did the commander receive a call from some local official of the SDG in Bijeljina; and if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the call from Biljana Plavsic, there was contact -- contact was established with our people in Bijeljina. And our member whose nickname is Mauzer told us that it was absolutely necessary for the guards to go and liberate Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After your arrival there, did you find out from Arkan or from someone else, did you find out whether the guards participated in the liberation of Bijeljina on an independent basis, or were they provided with support of some kind? And if so, with what kind of support?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The guards had two forms of support. They were supported by our members led by Mauzer. I can't remember his name right now, but the nickname, his nickname, is Mauzer. But the main form of support was in the form of logistics, and it was provided by the army, an army garrison in Bijeljina. Major Gavrilovic commanded that garrison and he later became the commander of the 2nd Semberija Brigade. Our volunteers slept in the barracks and that's where they would also eat for the day or two that they spent there. So the army provided us with logistics support, but the agreement was that the army should provide us with full combat support as well. But since we co-operated very successfully with the local patriots and groups, it wasn't necessary for the Army of Yugoslavia to get involved in the conflict. They remained in the barracks. So in one day's time Bijeljina was liberated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could please have a little bit more foundation. It started out with the witness not being present for any of this, then went into that he subsequently heard about things, and now things are coming in to the record in a conclusory fashion as if the witness almost experienced these directly. So if we could have please a little bit more foundation on how he learned this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, it may be -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just going to ask the witness precisely that. I was just going to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, it seems to me that you had a coded letter in your hands. Could you please provide us with some more details? Who did you receive the information from? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that. My initial office originates from my colleagues, volunteers, as soon as I returned from the Krka monastery sometimes toward the end of April. I had been there with four of the other volunteers in order to protect the monastery. Later on, when I became close associate of Commander Arkan, in that capacity and later on as a politician I met with Biljana Plavsic and all the other relevant people from the Republika Srpska. Obviously I wanted to know how things had happened, and this is what I base my very reliable information on, the -- the one that I share with the Honourable Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, did Arkan speak openly about all those details? In the media, for example.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on many occasion, because that was most frequently a journalist's questions during that period. Later on I became Major Gavrilovic's friend. Unfortunately, he died a few months ago. However, from various sources I heard what had caused our attack on Bijeljina, how things evolved and what the result was, so I believe that I have all the relevant information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The transport is not -- the transcript is not clear. It doesn't reflect what you said about Major Gavrilovic. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: When Major Gavrilovic became the commander of the 2nd Brigade, we met and we became good friends, and it is only logical that I asked him how things happened in Bijeljina, because there were several versions about the events. And I also spoke on several occasions with Mauzer who remained living in Bijeljina and established his own guard under the name of Panthers. I collected all information from different sources, and I was able to put together the picture of what had happened in Bijeljina. It was not difficult at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, now I'm going to show you three photos. And in the meantime, I would kindly ask the booths to prepare firstly the transcript for 2D1008.1. Before that, I would like to call up 2D1028, which is a photo that we received from you, Mr. Pelevic -- Mr. Pelevic, I apologise. Let me ask you, Mr. Pelevic, do you know anything about the circumstances under which the Serbian Volunteer Guard and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, participated in the Zvornik operation in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I will have to say that I was not there. I was not one of the participants. But I have information that came from different sources. During the operation in Bijeljina, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina sent a delegation to investigate what had happened there. The delegation consisted of Biljana Plavsic, Fikret Abdic, and General Prascevic on behalf of the military. According to Biljana Plavsic, according to what she told me later and according what her statements for the media were, the situation in Bijeljina was good. No shop was looted. Wherever a shop window glass was broken, Commander Arkan posted a guard there to guard such shops. Commander Arkan wanted to proceed and attack Tuzla; however, Vladika Vasilije Kacevenda talked him out of that. He was also present there, as well as Biljana Plavsic. General Prascevic claimed that the situation in Tuzla was under control and no attacks could ensue from there from any of the peoples residing there. So the idea was given up on, and Biljana Plavsic insisted on proceeding towards Zvornik, where the Serbs came under the threat of the Muslim forces that had organised themselves just like they had done in Bijeljina. And that's how a decision was made to proceed towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know, did you hear from Arkan or anybody else, who participated in the Zvornik operation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the Serbian Volunteers Guard consisting of some 60 volunteers or so - because it would have been impossible for only 60 volunteers to take Zvornik, Zvornik is a somewhat larger town - we acted in concert with the Army of Yugoslavia. And I believe that the main commander was General Sava Jankovic. I know that for a fact. I don't know who was the operative in charge of the operation, but I know that the guards enjoyed artillery and infantry support, but the artillery support was decisive in the attack to liberate Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, please look at the photo 2D1028 which is before you. Do you know who the photo depicts? What was the occasion when the photo was taken, and when?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The photo was taken in 1995 on the anniversary of the MUP of Serbia on the day of Archangel Mikajla," and the person at the roster is Radovan Karadzic, the then-president of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, there is an error in the transcript. What MUP anniversary?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The MUP of the Republika Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: It was in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at another photo, which is 2D1029.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, can you tell us when this photo was taken and what it depicts?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The photo was taken in Zvornik on the same day, on the same occasion, in Zvornik. This is Commander Arkan, and the other person is an official of the MUP. He was present -- Arkan was presented with a gift. I don't know who the official was. But I know that this is a pistol with an engraving, a dedication to Arkan as the liberator of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that he received that gift from an official of what institution?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The MUP of the Republika Srpska. It was their anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's look at 2D1026. Could you please identify the event. Tell us whether the photo depicts the same event. And can you please identify the four individuals, starting from the right-hand side of the photo towards the left.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The first one on the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The event is the same, 1995, the anniversary of the MUP of Republika Srpska. The first person on the right is the minister of the police of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Tomislav Kovac. Second is Radovan Karadzic, the president of the Republika Srpska. The first [as interpreted] individual is Vladika Vasilije Kacevenda. And the fourth person is Commander Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the three exhibits, 2D1028, 2D1029, and 2D1026, be tendered into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the present photo, I see the witness has identified through to Zeljko Raznjatovic but did not -- we do not know whether or not he also recognises the other individuals along sitting in that row.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could ask him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. With that being said, also we do not how this witness has personal knowledge of this event. Did he attend, is this something that he saw on TV, or whatnot? Provided that there's personal knowledge established by this witness, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the numbers would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1028 will receive number D652. Document 2D1029 will receive number D653. And document 2D1026 whether receive number D654, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in view to them being very much related, Madam Registrar, is there any specific reason why we would have them under three numbers rather than as three photographs from the anniversary?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are uploaded as separated documents. I cannot merge them without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether that's logic or not, I leave that apart. But D652 up to and including D654 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, we received several photos and we made a selection. We did not want to encumber the file with too many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Things are as they are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, please be so kind and tell us where us got the photos from. Were you present at the event? How do you know about the event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we know, until now, is that photographs with a rather clearer explanation on a screen, what it was about, that it was the MUP, the year is there. The witness wasn't there. He recognises the persons. I would have been able to recognise most of them as well, I think, on the basis of the existing evidence. What now is the line of questioning? What are you going to further establish, I wonder, Mr. Bakrac? "How do you know about the event?" Is there is any dispute about the event taking place in view of ... and what is the major relevance to know -- I see -- I take it the point is that Arkan is seen in the presence of Republika Srpska officials, Mr. Karadzic. He even got a present. That is, I take it, the purpose of all of this is, to link Mr. Arkan to Republika Srpska, as often in the Defence strategy it seems that linking Arkan to the JNA, linking Arkan to the Republika Srpska MUP, is apparently something you want to establish. Now, what will -- the questions how the witness is aware of this, if -- I don't know there's much dispute about it, but I'm really asking myself where are we going to end, and is it of such importance that we should pay a lot of attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Weber reacted and suggested that we should establish how he knows about the photos is what prompted me. And second of all, we had a protected witness in this courtroom who testified that in 1995 Arkan was not very welcome in the territory of Republika Srpska, that -- that he had been chased away, as it were. Now we are trying to establish what Arkan's relationship was with the Republika Srpska officials, and we're trying to challenge some of the allegations presented by the witnesses in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's clear. I think that you can see in the photographs that it was -- apparently this meeting was held in Zvornik, if I'm not mistaken. And if I remember well, 1995 appears there as the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're having a longer discussion than what I intended. The reason was, the contents of the photos is not why I said something about the personal knowledge and foundation, it was that he was offering details beyond what the photos were. So if it was just a matter of the content of the photos, as Your Honours have noticed, that would not been -- that would not have initiated the comment that I made in terms of the personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Keep all this in the back of your mind, Mr. Bakrac, and then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm looking at the clock. I believe that we are already on the break time, and maybe this would be a convenient moment, because after the break I have some other video-clips to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are. And we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Bakrac, I was informed by the Registry that the video, without sound, you wanted to tender still has not been received by the Registry in such a form that it can be processed. And that's the only reason why I have not yet assigned not even a provisional number to it. You should take care that it is received by the Registrar in such a way that it can be processed in the system. Then, Mr. Bakrac --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we were speaking about a certain subject matter. I would now like to conclude. Tell me, before -- after you returned from Krka, and after the operations in Bijeljina and Zvornik, did any officials from Republika Srpska visit your camp in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In May, I believe, Ms. Biljana Plavsic went to Erdut, together with Princess Linda Karadjordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we now have a look at 2D1020. Could we have that document up on the screen. It's a photograph that we received from the witness. Could you please zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Going from left to right, could you tell us who is sitting in this room? And could you tell us when and where this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: This photograph was taken a little time after the operation in Bijeljina and Zvornik. I think it was in May, but I'm not certain. It was taken in the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guards in Erdut, and it was taken in Commander Arkan's office. I can't recognise the first gentleman to the left. Ms. Biljana Plavsic is sitting next to him. Princess Linda Karadjordjevic, who is the wife of Prince Tomislav Karadjordjevic, is sitting next to Ms. Plavsic. The gentleman to her left is someone I can't recognise, and the person in uniform is Commander Arkan. The gentleman with the beard, to the extreme right, is someone I can recognise but I can't remember his name. I know it's a politician from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, but I do not know exactly what his name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you present on the occasion of this visit?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I was the person who took the photograph with the authorisation of the guards' commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On that occasion were any previous operations were discussed; and, if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Because at the time I was just a junior officer and I could not attend the meeting. And, therefore, I do not know what was discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this photograph, 2D1020, please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1020 will receive number D655, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
