utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, upon returning from Krajina, from the Krka monastery, you said you returned to Erdut and that this was towards the end of April 1992. Tell us, very briefly, what you continued to do and where you stayed until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I continued to train the guards. On the whole, I was involved in my own activities. I was in an office, I had premises there. In the meantime, I was conferred the rank officer and I had my own room. In the morning I trained the Serbian Volunteer Guards. I trained them to be physically fit. I trained them in the martial arts. And in the afternoon I trained the troops how to use Zoljas, hand-held rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, at some point in time did you cease to provide training for the volunteers; and if that was the case, what was the reason? And when did you cease providing such training?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Since I was noticed as an officer by Commander Arkan, in the meantime I was promoted. And as a co-driver, he wanted me to be with him all the time when he was in the jeep. He didn't have a driver and he drove himself, so I would sit by his side. Sometime in November, when we had a brief break and were in Belgrade, he called me to his office, at his exchange office that he in the centre of Belgrade, and he showed me a list with about 20.000 signatures of the citizens of Serbian nationality, citizens from Kosovo and Metohija, and these citizens had asked him to present himself as a candidate, as a national deputy from Kosovo and Metohija. He asked me what I thought about that. I tried to dissuade him. I said it wasn't difficult to be a national representative, a member of parliament. I said that it was a far greater honour to be a commander within the Serbian Volunteer Guards. Since I didn't have any interest in politics up until then, I wanted to persuade him not to get involved in politics. He said that he had already taken his decision and that he wanted me to be the second person on his list when presenting himself for that position. I refused to comply with the request. I said I was an economist and that I was not interested in politics. He was angry, but he had a -- a special relationship with me, and he would never raise his voice, nor would he do anything that I would hold against him. I left. On the following day, the secretary called me, his secretary Snezana Kalinic called me. She asked for my identity card so that she could register me on the -- in the files of the Serbian Volunteer Guards. I provided my identity card to the courier who came to my house, and 15 days later my name appeared in the newspapers in the mid-section and I was the second person on the list of the group of citizens that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, the group of citizens from Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting you, Mr. Pelevic. We have a limited amount of time. I would like to confine myself to what we are interested in, in the courtroom. I do have to interrupt you in order to focus on what we are interested in. As far as I have understood, you became a candidate for the group of citizens led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and you were the second person on his list. What did you do up until that point in time? How long did that campaign take?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of continuity, I will briefly say that I was angry when I read this in the newspaper, but later he persuaded me that this was for the best. I accepted that as a fact. We started our campaign in the towns of Kosovo and Metohija. I was practically in charge of the campaign. And we did very well in the elections. We received a lot of votes and obtained five seats in the parliament of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Be so kind as to tell me who financed that campaign.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't an expensive campaign, since only a few towns were concerned. There were meetings that were held in sports halls. Usually these halls would be provided to us by the directors for free. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, financed all the expenses incurred by the campaign, but the expenses were not that significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I was waiting for the interpretation to avoid overlapping speakers. When were the elections held? And out of those -- amongst those five members of parliament, were you one of them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I think the elections were concluded in December 1992. I became a member of parliament. Since we had five seats, we could have our own group. Mr. Raznjatovic was the president of the parliamentary group, and I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Before we move on, Mr. Pelevic, we were speaking about the financing of the campaign. Could you briefly explain the following for me: How did the Serbian Volunteer Guards finance itself?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as supplies were concerned, we would receive everything from the TO for free and also from companies in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. There were factories and companies that provided supplies for us. But there were also companies, some companies, from Vojvodina, from Serbia, that were in the vicinity of the border of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, so that wasn't a problem. I've already told you how we obtained weapons and ammunition. So these were the financial sources for the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard receive salaries?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't, with the exception of a few officials who worked in Belgrade, who worked in the recruitment office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We'll return to that issue later on. So, in December you became a member of parliament in the Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we now please see the following video-clip: 2D1001.1. It's a 65 ter document, V000-0268, it's a Prosecution number. The Prosecution has already shown a part of the speech given by Mr. Raznjatovic. The speech lasts five minutes. I want to see the end of the speech, too, because I have a few questions about that. The Prosecution has already shown this speech about uniting Serbian territories, so I would like to have a look at the entire video-clip, which will take five minutes, and then I will have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "How do Serbs greet each other? Americans have their American dream, the French have a French dream, the Italians have an Italian dream. We, the Serbs, also have the right to dream. So do I. I have my own dream and you have your own Serbian dream, and that relates to the united Serbian territory. "You have seen that Germany has united, although it inflicted an incredible evil of the population of the entire world and on us Serbs in particular. They united. No one objected to that. So why do they object to us uniting in one -- within one state? Because we are one people, we speak one language, and we have the right to the united states of Serbia. "I returned from Kosovo this morning. Last night I was in Djakovica where I had a promotion in front of 1.200 Serbs. Those were all the Serbs who remained in Djakovica and they gathered in that hall. Half of the hall was crying when I gave my speech because those people down there have no hope. Albanian mercenaries cross the border there and loot and rape Serbian women, and the police force there is unable to protect them. So they are seeking the protection of the Serbian volunteers. "In the Serbian Republic of Krajina, you know where Jovanovac is, Ustasha forces are amassing there. There are Leopard armoured tank units, but they can't cross the border there because of the special police units in Krajina but also because of the Serbian Tigers who won't allow the perpetration of another genocide against the Serbian people. The children should sleep peacefully. The working people should continue to work, because we are watching over them and we will be the first to intervene and close the gaps should the enemy make a move from any direction. We won't allow the Ustasha and fascist monsters to swallow our children again, to devour our children again. In Bosnia we prevented there being a border on the Drina river. The force of the Jihad had already occupied Bijeljina. Everything was already in their hands when we arrived and got rid of the Jihad. We are afraid of no one. "The only thing we fear is a lack of unity among the Serbs. For this reason, my brothers, I want to appeal to Serbian unity at this honourable and honest gathering. Let's not tarnish our image. We don't need that. We know that among the Serbs there have always been people, but there have been others who didn't deserve such a name. But we know how to deal with such animals. That might be harsh on my part. Perhaps I'm not yet politically correct, and I do apologise, I am not yet a member of the parliament. But I do have to tell you one thing. And that is that there can be no mention of trade with Serbian lands or Serbian people. I'm saying this here and now. "Nobody can play games with the Serbian 'inteligencija,' with Serbian intelligence, no one can offer you thousands of German marks. Where does that money come from? Let me tell you. They wish to sell Kosovo. They wish to sell the Krajinas. Well, we won't allow it. We won't give them Krajina or Kosovo. "Kosovo and the Krajinas and all the Serbian lands are sacred, because our churches are located there. Our homesteads are there, our graves are there, and we won't give up a single inch of that territory. "The politicians can remain involved in politics, but they need to know that we will not be trading with Serbian lands or Serbian people. The Serbian people will not allow it. They have to know that. So I greet you from this stand, here today, my brothers. "Thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, this was a somewhat longer clip, but I wanted to hear the entire speech. We heard Mr. Raznjatovic mentioning a discord among the Serbs. At one point he said they want to sell Serbian Krajinas and the Serbian Kosovo. Can you tell us, if you know, since you participated in the campaign, who did Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, refer to when he has says -- he said "they want to sell the Serbian Krajinas"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: It is very clear that he meant the politicians in power, because there was nobody else who was in a position to trade in Serbian Krajinas and Serbian Kosovo and Metohija but the powers that be. It was a direct attack on Slobodan Milosevic and his policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the then-official politicians and institution support Arkan's public efforts in the sense of uniting all Serbian lands?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No. The powers that be did not want the unification of all Serb lands. As Mr. Raznjatovic said, we dreamt about that. We had the right to dream. But it was only a dream. And later on it turned out that he was right when it came to the sale of Krajina, and with that I mean the Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. The -- and the -- today's power is doing the same thing with Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, can you please tell us about the gathering that we saw. When did that take place? Who was present? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: That gathering was part of the election campaign. It was at the Sava conference hall, possibly November, perhaps December; it doesn't really matter. I was there as the only one representing our party, and both him and I spoke at that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said November or December. What year? And what was the official title of that rally? Were there any other officials there? Was there anybody there from any of the Serbian Krajinas? And if that was the case, who were they?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I said that it was either in November or December, I'm not sure, but it was 20 years ago, and you really can't expect me to remember everything really precisely. That was at the Sava centre conference hall. It was a Serbian rally of sorts. Officials came from the Republika Srpska, from the republic of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could I stop you there. The first question was: "What year?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] November or December 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that officials came from the Republika Srpska, and you wanted to continue.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Republic of Serbian Krajina, Montenegro, and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you remember who represented the Republika Srpska, who represented the Republic of Serbian Krajina, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember any of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic. When you became an MP, were you in coalition with Milosevic's party, or were you a member of the opposition?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: After Zeljko Raznjatovic's speak [as interpreted] at that Serbian rally, all we could expect were attacks from the government. We could not expect them to invite us to form a coalition. In the parliament we were opposition to the Socialist Party of Serbia headed by Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you enjoy support from the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina? And if there was support, what kind of support was that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: This was just a campaign. We still didn't know whether we would make it to the parliament when we did. We established very good political connections with the officials of both the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Not because they respected our political work, we were novices in that, but they respected our fight for the liberation of the Serbian territories in both Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and that's what we based our good relationship with the then-politicians of those two regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, you started engaging in politics when you became an MP. Was there another mobilisation drive of the Serbian Volunteer Guards? And if that was the case, when and where?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Volunteer Guards were never disbanded. However, the two of us started dedicating our time to political world. Towards the end of January, the Croatian forces started attacking Maslenica and numerous crimes were committed against innocent population. Unfortunately, this was happening in front of the peacekeeping forces of the United Nations. And then we departed for Erdut. Commander Arkan and myself went to Erdut. We put on our uniforms once again and joined the Serbian Volunteer Guard on a campaign towards the Knin-Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, when you were supposed to cross the border from Erdut, you said that you joined the guards. I suppose that you're talking about a large number of people. How did you organise that? How did you do that? How did you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: From before, there was agreement in place between Commander Arkan and minister of defence of the Army of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Tomislav Simovic, according to which we were allowed to use military trucks and according to which we would not be crossing the border at the official border crossing, but, rather, that we would use some military routes. That's how we crossed the border from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem onto the territory of the Republika Srpska and into the Knin-Krajina. It would have not been possible any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, I would like us to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said, Mr. Pelevic, "towards the end of January," may I take it that you were referring to January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to call up 2D1036.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, while we're waiting for the document, let me tell you that this seems to be an intercept that the Croatian side intercepted on the 4th of May, 1995. You say that with a large number of soldiers you left Erdut to go to the Knin-Krajina. I would be interested whether the principle that we see here functioned even before this time. We can look at the document where we can see that around 2210 hours Major Vrudin [phoen], commander of the 35th Brigade, who, on the meeting with General Loncar, ordered to Captain Cedo Jovic, chief of the security of the 35th Brigade, to close all the border crossings at the 24 hours on the 4th of May, 2005, between the so-called SRY and the so-called RSK and that he could only allow the passage of one Arkan's unit of an unknown strength which had already been announced to us before. Your Honour, can I see Mr. Weber on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There's an objection to the characterisation of this document that's been posed to the witness. It's the Prosecutor's understanding that these documents are summaries that were provided by the Croatian government of intercepts that are in their possession, so it doesn't reflect the actual content of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know whether it reflects the actual content. It is a summary which is either accurate or inaccurate, but it certainly does not reflect all the words spoken by the interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just providing to the Chamber the information that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to check with the witness whether this procedure or a similar procedure was well established when the Serbian Volunteer Guard had to move from Erdut to go to a theatre of war. 2D1035 is proof that the intercept was provided by the Croatian authorities to the OTP pursuant to a Request for Assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not ask a question to the witness, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, whatever -- this apparently is a contemporaneous document provided by the Croatians, at least it's presented as such. Is there any problem in using it? Apart from that it is a summary of what apparently was either intercepted -- what was intercepted most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, we do object to it. This is a form of leading. This information as for what Mr. Bakrac has said it was used for could have been lead without even the use of a document. Secondly, Mr. Bakrac said that the Croatian authorities provided the OTP, pursuant to a Request for Assistance, the intercept. We do not have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have various matters. First, Mr. Bakrac, Mr. Weber says that you should have tried to elicit this, the answers from the witness, without first showing him what was said during this intercept. And I think that would be in accordance with -- with the instructions, certainly if it is a witness have you called yourself. The other questions, the other issues raised; one is that you did not adequately present the document, and third, that the Prosecution has no access to the original transcript. Would that make this document inadmissible under all circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the context that it's being offered today, we would object. I mean, that's not to say that further investigations couldn't be done and such information couldn't be admissible in other forms, but the way it's being used today with this witness, yes, we would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear the answers of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be allowed, I did not even mean to tender it through this witness. I simply want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... earlier I said: "Why not ask a question to the witness." Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, before we looked at the document, I asked you how you crossed, and you told us that there was an agreement between Simovic and Arkan about military trucks and so on and so forth. And you said that you crossed the border somewhere else and not across the official crossings. What I've just read out, does it reflect the way the Serbian Volunteer Guards crossed the border to go from Erdut to other theatres of war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: There was an agreement in principle between Arkan and the minister of defence of Serbia according to which we crossed in this way. However, the implementation of this agreement was in the hands of the authorised organs of the Army of Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Army of Yugoslavia. And this was precisely in order to avoid police checks, because our people could not travel through the Republic of Serbia or they could not cross where there were police checks. That's why we wanted to avoid police controls. We used military routes while all the other crossings were closed so that we could pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic. When you arrived in the Knin-Krajina in January 1993, where were you billeted? Did you participate in any of the operations there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: We were billeted in Benkovac, in Aseria [phoen] hotel, which had been completely empty. There was no food to be had. We had problem with food -- food supplies. We participated in some operations around Benkovac, on the Paljuv plateau, where there are several Serbian villages that had been plundered and torched. Islam Grcki and Islam Latinski and some other villages where the population had suffered terribly, and there is UN documentation to prove that. Later on there was struggle to liberate Maslenica and the Serbian volunteers actively participated in that fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that the Serbian Volunteer Guards actively participated in those military operations, could you please tell us, Under whose command did the Serbian volunteers operate at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Since the Serbian Volunteer Guards from the very outset was under the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and then when the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established, it became part of that Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It was only all normal for them to be under the command of the commander of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that was Mile Novakovic, and we did that when we fought in the Knin and Benkovac theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that from the very outset you were under the command of the TEO [as interpreted] and that later on at the beginning of 1993 you were members of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. In the meantime between 1991 and 1993, January 1993, were there any changes with regard to your affiliation? And if such changes did take place, when was that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a change in 1992 after the adoption of Cyrus Vance's peace plan according to which both warring parties should be without militaries. Pursuant to an order that we received from the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, we were transformed into the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and we operated in that way up to the attack on Maslenica in late January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When we're talking about these operations around Maslenica in January 1993, you said you were under the command of Mile Novakovic. In addition to your forces, were there any other forces from the MUP of the Republic of Serbia or the DB of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No. There were only Wolves from Vucjak from the Republika Srpska under the command of the late Veljko Milankovic and some other units from the Army of Republika Srpska with us. But the bulk of the forces were from the Republic of Serbian Krajina, including the Serbian Volunteer Guards, as its integral element.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you wounded at that time? And if that was the case, could you please describe what happened? How were you wounded and what happened next.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: According to a plan that was drafted by the command, the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the Serbian Volunteer Guards were designated to pave the road across Velebit and come to Srebrenica. On our flank were several units from the Republika Srpska and the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I was the commander of that company that launched a frontal attack. After two attacks, I was wounded by a -- a bullet that was -- that is banned by the Geneva Conventions. I was wounded in the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, if I could just take you and perhaps the witness back a tinny little bit. You read the content of the summary of the intercept. You read, at least that is how it's reflected in the transcript, that all the border crossings would be closed between the so-called, as it reads in our transcript, "SFRY," and the so-called RSK. Now, the original, at least the translation, also, I think, in B/C/S says "SRJ," which is not the same as the SFRY. First of all, could you perhaps read "SRJ" but then not using the acronym. SRJ stands for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I apologise if I made a mistake when reading it out. The original says the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then we have an acronym, and the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But SRJ, if it's not the federal republic, is it the -- what is it, that, in full? The so-called SRJ stands for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time in 1995, and somewhat earlier, when the republics of Slavonia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina were recognised, as well as the republic of Macedonia, Serbia and Montenegro remained, and these two entities were called the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it consisted of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings me exactly to my point where I'm totally confused about the evidence given by this witness. The witness explained to us, and please listen carefully, that the -- you explained that you came from Belgrade, went to Erdut. From Erdut you had to finally reach the Republic of Serbian Krajina. May I take it that that was the Republic of Serbia Krajina which was on -- well, let's say, on Croatian territory, or at least what used to be Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the Republic of Serbia Krajina, but correct me when I'm wrong, was partly found in what used to be Croatian territory. That is, Serbian Krajina, Knin area, that area. Are you referring to that, or are you referring to any other part of the Republic of Serbia Krajina. You are referring to the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you explained to us that there was a special arrangement with the -- for crossing borders with the ... and that was a agreement between Commander Arkan and the minister of defence of the army of the Republic of Serbia. You also explained that you would take a route through Republika Srpska and then go to the Republika Srpska Krajina. Would that mean crossing the border from Erdut first into Republika Srpska and then into the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We had to travel for a brief period through the republic -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And this agreement concerned that stretch, and not the trip from Republika Srpska to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was never a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now the document you've shown to the witness is about border crossings between the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia and the so-called Republic of Serb Krajina. Which border are we now -- who is moving from where to where exactly? And what -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I know what the situation was like, and if I may interpret what the witness has just said, because of the front line -- well, I do apologise. To avoid any mistakes, I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was it possible to go from Erdut to the Republic of Serbian Krajina to Knin without passing through the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or, rather, through Serbia, through part of that federal entity?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't possible because it would have required passing through Croatian territory, which is where the Croatian forces were present, and that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that that agreement was to go from Erdut back into Serbia and then from Serbia into the Republika Srpska and from the Republika Srpska into the Republika Srpska Krajina. That is what that agreement is about, isn't it? Well, at least the first stretch -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. Going from Erdut to Serbia and then Serbia to Republika Srpska was the problem. But the witness said that it wasn't a problem to go from Republika Srpska to the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now, the document shown related to the telephone intercept is crossings between the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia and the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina. Now, from what I understood is that from Erdut you'd go to the Republic of Serbia, then you would cross the border with the Republika Srpska, and from the Republika Srpska, then to Republika Srpska Krajina. So I'm wondering where do I find border crossings between the SRJ and the RSK? Where do I find them? Because I understand that it was Erdut, crossing the border to Serbia, from Serbia to Republika Srpska, from Republika Srpska to the Republika of Srpska Krajina. So I'm -- I have border crossings between two states which are not neighbouring each other. SRJ and the RSK. In between there is the Republika Srpska. So I'm asking myself how to understand this document at all. I'm just trying to understand the geography, and that's the reason why I -- although I had -- of course, I -- I expected that where you -- you misread or it was missed -- where it was not accurately put on the transcript, the SRJ, because I wanted that to be clarified first before I could put this question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the northern part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that northern part which shares a border with the Republic of Serbian Krajina, is Serbia. To the south we have Montenegro, which didn't share a border with the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And then these crossings were crossings between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but it was in the territory of Serbia. As far as I have understood the witness's testimony, they weren't border crossings but military crossings. These were military routes that they used, but they passed through the territory of Serbia to a certain extent. And the territory of Serbia was an integral part of the state that was known as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you say in the northern part there is a border between the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, it being Serbia there, and the Serbian Krajina, you are referring to, could I say, the eastern part of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the eastern part. And the west and part of Serbia or, rather, of the SRJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you are actually -- what, then, the evidence is, and now I think I understand it better, that moving from the eastern part, Western Slavonia, Srem, that area, to the other part of the Republika Srpska Krajina, you would have to cross through Croatian-held territory, and that was the reason why from the Republika Srpska Krajina, although the eastern part, you would move to Serbia, then to the Republic of -- Republika Srpska, and then -- so -- and then finally to the western part of the Republika Srpska Krajina. So when we are looking this document, it is the border crossing between Serbia proper and the eastern part of the social republic -- of the Serbian Republic Krajina -- Republika Srpska Krajina, I'm sorry. What confused me, of course, is that often we are referring to "We go to Erdut," but Erdut was Republika Srpska Krajina but only the eastern part. So to say to go from Erdut and reach the Republika Srpska Krajina is, to that extent, nonsense, that it is already part of the Republika Srpska Krajina, although we are talking about going to another sector or another part of the Republika Srpska Krajina. I think it's now all perfectly clear to me. But could we please -- if we use those words, "we go to Erdut" or "we go to the -- from Erdut to the RSK," is, of course, if Erdut is already part of the RSK, what the exact wording should have been is: "We go from Erdut to the western part of the Republika Srpska Krajina and in order to reach that western part, we would have to go through Serbia, Republika Srpska, and then cross that border." The language used is not consistent. And I would -- in order not to be confused, apart from small inaccuracies in the transcript, again, I do not know what you read. I think, as a matter of fact, that you did read "SRJ," but I leave that alone. It's now perfectly clear to me again. And could we always, if we are referring to places, then we are referring to places. If we are referring to geographical entities, that we give them the proper name. That is, in this case, going to Republika Srpska Krajina, to the western part of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand, and I will make an effort to put precise questions so that we don't get confused about these stretches of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, very briefly. You said you were seriously wounded in the battle-field. Where were you transported to and how long were you treated for?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: From the top of Velebit I was taken to Mali Alan. There was an HQ there. And then I was taken to the hospital in Gracac, they couldn't intervene there. And then I was taken to the Sveti Save hospital in Knin, from Knin by helicopter to Banja Luka, and from Banja Luka after two days I was transported in an ambulance to the VM -- the military medical academy in Belgrade, since there were no flights between Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a result of an order issued by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why were you transported to the VMU -- VMA in Belgrade in order to be treated there, the military and medical academy?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: That was agreement between Arkan and the minister of defence of the Army of Yugoslavia. The agreement was that our wounded should be taken to the VMA where they would be treated. Or sometimes, because the VMA didn't have the capacity, some soldiers would be taken elsewhere. But most of the soldiers, and that included myself, were provided with treatment at the military and medical academy, the VMA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did members of the SDG -- were the welfare certificates taken to the MUP in Serbia in order to be checked? Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the Serbian MUP or DB ever certify the welfare certificates of your soldiers in order to provide them with treatment?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No. Why? That was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic. Mr. Pelevic, when your treatment had been completed, where did you return to and what did you do after you returned there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: My treatment still hasn't been completed, but three months later I was already capable of continuing to work. I returned to the Serbian parliament as a national member of parliament, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And throughout the year 1993 you were involved in politics in parliament; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1993 were new elections held? And if that was the case, did you participate in them? And in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. President Milosevic called an election that was held, I believe, towards the end of the year. In December 1993, I believe. We participated in the election. We first founded a political party called the Party for Serbian Unity, and this was done in accordance with what the president of the party, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, stated in a video-clip. We continue to be involved in policies and as a party we participated in those parliamentary elections. These were preliminary parliamentary elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us at that time towards the end of 1993 what results did you obtain at the elections? Did you manage to enter parliament?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, that was not the case, and we believe that we were the subject of deception at those elections. The votes had been stolen from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you reach the threshold at all that was necessary to enter parliament?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No. Because the leading party didn't want the Party of Serbian Unity to enter parliament. There are indications that many of our votes had been stolen at those elections by the leading party that was led by Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you and Mr. Raznjatovic talk about being close to the MUP, the DB? And if had you been close to them, would you have passed threshold? Did you ever talk about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: No, not in that way. But we realized that we were in the way of the ruling party and Slobodan Milosevic and that's why we didn't make it to the parliament. If we teamed up with his party, if we subscribed to his policies, we would have certainly made it to the parliament. Not only that, we would have probably won many more votes than we did during the first elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: During the pre-election campaigns in 1993, did Arkan talk to Badza? Was he in contact with Badza? What was their relationship? What kind of contacts did they have?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: His connections with Badza were still friendly but Badza was never involved in politics. So whatever conversations they had, they were not political conversations they were not -- they didn't deal with the campaign. Those were military conversations dealing with the status of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Having lost in the elections in December 1993, having not made it to the parliament, in early 1994 did you participate in any war activities? Were there any such activities at all?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the beginning of that year? No. There were no important war activities at the time. We continued pursuing our political work. We were determined to improve our political rating. However, at the rallies that we held all over Serbia, we realized that our popularity was already very strong and we were even more deeply concerned after that that we had lost in the elections unjustly, because the votes had been stolen from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, the territorial centre in Erdut, did it continue to operate in 1994? And if that was the case, until when did it operate?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: It continued to operate in the beginning of that year up to the end of March or the beginning of April. And then we were moved from there. The guards had not been disbanded as such, but they were all on a long furlough. However, each guard member was obliged to respond to the commander's call.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that the guard members were on a long furlough, can you tell us when was that? From when to when?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: The guards became passive. The whole organisation became passive. And that passivity lasted for a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My colleague is signalling to me that something is not clear in the transcript. Let's finish with that. We have two more minutes. If I understood you properly, the camp in Erdut remained open sometime until the end of March and the beginning of April 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then you said that the organisation became passive and the members of the guards were on a long furlough. Until when? How long did that last for?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: A few months. I can't tell you exactly how long. It was a long time ago, so I can't be sure of any of the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are we talking about 1994 still?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So am I, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Pelevic, we will adjourn for the day. And we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom. But before we adjourn, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony or communicate in any other way, written or oral, about your testimony, whether that is it testimony you've given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. Another question I would raise: Mr. Bakrac, could you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had not make the same mistake again. Last time I had an old estimate. I know that we envisaged four hours for this witness. I don't know how much I spent, but, with your leave, I would ask for another hour and a half tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would fit within your original estimate. So shortly after the first break you would conclude your examination-in-chief. We adjourn. And we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 25th of January, at 9.00 in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of January, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
